items.title: Before you begin
items.body:
Learn about Pass Functional Skills (PFS): what it is, who it's for, and how the product actually works.

Before you begin, take a few minutes to explore this [interactive, step-by-step walkthrough](https://app.supademo.com/demo/cmd37vg3i3kl9c4kjjvwlgdl3?step=1) of the Pass Functional Skills Maths Level 2 online course. It will give you a useful overview of the platform and help you become familiar with how the course works. Don't worry about exploring everything in detail at this stage, as Module 4 covers the course structure more thoroughly. For now, just use it to gain some initial context before starting your learning journey.

items.title: Module 1: Introduction to Pass Functional Skills (PFS)
items.body:
**Some of this will be familiar from the Pre-Interview Foundations course. This first module is a quick refresher and introduction to Pass Functional Skills (PFS).**

## What is PFS?

Pass Functional Skills (PFS) offers Functional Skills qualifications in maths and English. We offer Entry Level 3, Level 1, and Level 2. It is regulated by Ofqual, so it is accredited and recognised by universities, apprenticeship providers, training providers, and employers.

## The levels: Entry Level 3 up to Level 2

PFS offers Functional Skills maths and English across three levels: Entry Level 3, Level 1, and Level 2. Entry Level 3 is foundational, below GCSE. Level 1 is roughly old GCSE grades 1–3 (D–G). Level 2 is the top and equivalent to a GCSE grade 4 (grade C) — what most customers need, as it's the level nurses, universities, and apprenticeships usually ask for. Always confirm the level a learner's route actually requires rather than assuming Level 2.

## Subjects we offer

Functional Skills exists in three subjects only: maths, English, and digital skills. PFS provides the full end-to-end service (course + exam) for maths and English, from Entry Level 3 up to Level 2. For Digital Skills we offer a course-only option at Level 1.

## How it's delivered

The course is studied online from home, at the learner's own pace. The exam is also sat online; there is no paper-based option; and exams run 24/7, 365 days a year. For maths and English, the course and exam can be purchased together or separately; digital skills is course-only.

## Functional Skills vs. a real GCSE

Many learners assume they need a full GCSE when they don't. For maths or English, we usually recommend Functional Skills instead: it's online, from home, available 24/7/365, lower in cost, and uses practical, real-world content. A real GCSE is sat in person at an exam centre on set dates only, costs more, and covers more academic content. We still offer the real GCSE through our sister brand Pass GCSE (PMG) for learners whose university or employer specifically requires it.

Module 2: Who Needs PFS - The Audience
items.body:
**Learn the five main customer types, what each needs PFS for, their buying motivation, and their most likely objection.**

PFS suits anyone who needs a recognised maths or English qualification and whose university, employer or training provider accepts Functional Skills. Five customer types make up the bulk of who we sell to, and each comes to us for slightly different reasons.

## Nursing & healthcare applicant

Nurses & other healthcare applicants are our biggest group by far. They typically need Level 2 maths or English to complete a nursing or healthcare application, and they need it quickly; a placement or course start date is usually driving them. The question they almost always ask is whether their university or employer will actually accept Functional Skills. Don't assume: some healthcare employers specifically ask for equivalency instead, so check the exact requirement before recommending PFS.

## University applicants

These learners need a maths or English qualification to meet a university entry requirement, where the institution accepts Functional Skills in place of a GCSE. They're often working to a UCAS or course deadline, which adds urgency. The main tension is acceptance: they're rarely certain FS will be recognised. We can help them check the requirement and confirm it's likely, but always be clear that the final decision rests with the university — we never guarantee acceptance, so encourage them to confirm directly with the institution before booking.

## Apprenticeship applicants

For apprentices aged 16–18, English and maths is a mandatory part of completing the apprenticeship if they don't already hold a suitable equivalent — the required level depends on the apprenticeship (often a minimum of Level 1, up to Level 2). For those aged 19+, it's optional and at the employer's discretion (since Feb 2025), so always confirm what the apprentice actually needs before selling. Functional Skills is the fastest and cheapest is the route to meet these qualifications. PMG is more expensive, takes longer, and may be overkill. Equivalency may not be accepted.

## Career changers

These learners are moving into a new role or sector and need a recognised maths or English qualification, often having left education some time ago. Their priorities are speed and cost: they want to qualify quickly, around work, without paying over the odds. This is usually a straightforward conversation, because PFS is the cheapest and quickest route we offer — online, from home, with the exam included. Lead with speed and value, and reassure them it's Ofqual regulated and recognised, since some worry a faster route means a lesser one.

## Home-educated learners and parents

Home-educated learners and parents want something recognised, flexible and done from home. A common question parents ask is whether holding our qualification means their child counts as being in full-time education. It doesn't, by itself — for that to be the case they must apply to their local authority for sign-off. What we can do is provide evidence that the learner is enrolled on the course to support that application.

Module 3: The 10 Key Selling Points
items.body:
**Learn the 10 headline selling points of PFS — every salesperson must know them cold.**

## 1. Speed of turnaround from booking to exam

Exams run 365 days a year, 24 hours a day, so a learner isn't waiting for months for a fixed sitting - useful for anyone working to a schedule

## 2. Speed of results

We are registered with three major awarding bodies and can pick the fastest. VQA (TQUK) is the quickest, with results in 1–6 working days, and we choose the board that gets the learner their result in time. Results can be in within just 2 working days.

## 3. Track your progress with course access

The dashboard shows course progress, current level, revision time required, and the steps to becoming 'ExamReady', so learners always know where they stand.

## 4. Ofqual regulated

Because the qualification is Ofqual regulated, it is accepted by universities, apprenticeships, and employers across the UK.

## 5. Course flexibility — self-paced

Online with 24/7 access; we recommend around 50 hours of study but it can be done as quickly or slowly as the learner likes, from home.

## 6. Price — lowest cost guaranteed

We offer the most competitive pricing on a like-for-like service, and significantly less than a real GCSE.

## 7. Free resit — with a premium bundle booking

The premium bundle includes one free resit (a full resit for math, a single component resit for English); the basic bundle and funded options do not.

## 8. Free demo for course and exam, for those who need it

A demo lets the learner see exactly what they're buying — course features and the exact system — which removed hesitation before they register.

## 9. We work with universities and training providers across multiple sectors

This direct relationship is reassurance that our qualifications are known and accepted, not an unknown online certificate.

## 10. Pass rates are 93% for those who complete the course

As long as the learner puts the effort in, they should pass — frame it honestly: the 93% is for learners who finish the course.

Module 4: How the Course Works
items.body:
**The learning journey from Initial Assessment to Mock Exams, and what "ExamReady" means.**

As you work through this module, refer back to the [interactive course demo](https://app.supademo.com/demo/cmd37vg3i3kl9c4kjjvwlgdl3?step=1) to help you visualise the features and sections being discussed.

## 1. Initial Assessment

This is the learner's starting point — a 30-minute diagnostic mini test that establishes the level they're currently working at and recommends where to begin within the course, so they start at the right point rather than wading through material that's too easy or too hard. It's a guide only, not a fixed judgment, so a learner shouldn't feel boxed in by the result. For a salesperson, this is a useful reassurance point on a call: the learner doesn't need to know their level upfront, the course works it out and starts them in the right place.

## Subject Knowledge Assessment (SKA)

Where the Initial Assessment finds the overall level, the SKA goes topic by topic — a short test with one question on each topic to pinpoint exactly which areas are strong and which need work. From the results it generates a Personal Learning Plan: a tailored list of recommended topics, shown in the recommended-topics bar and highlighted in purple across the course, each tracked as not started, in progress or completed. The learner can then choose how to use it — work through the entire course for full coverage, or focus only on the recommended topics to save time and target their weak areas. Like the practice questions, each SKA question is marked with both a written and a video solution, so even the diagnostic stage is a learning opportunity.

## Course learning material

The course is fully comprehensive — every topic that could appear in the exam is covered, so no other revision materials are needed, and learners can work through topics in any order. Each topic has the same three sections: *Revise* (written slides and real expert-tutor videos that get more in-depth as you go, with adjustable speed, captions and unlimited views), *Practice Questions* (multiple choice in easy, medium and hard, every answer marked with written and video solutions whether right or wrong, unlimited attempts), and *Topic Tests* (the step up — multi-part, exam-style questions with typed answers, auto-marked with written and video feedback).

## Mock Exams

Board-specific papers built to match the question types and structure of the learner's chosen exam, AI-marked by "Dr Clive" with instant feedback — marks gained, marks lost and model answers, even for essay-style English. Maths Level 2 has 60 full papers (40 board-specific, 20 general); English Level 2 has 39. There are two modes: *Practice* (no time limit, marked question by question for learning) and *Exam* (timed to the real exam and marked only at the end) — the closest thing to the real sitting.

## ExamReady

The dashboard's objective signal that a learner is genuinely prepared, rather than a guess. It tracks progress live: course completion, current level and the revision time still needed. A learner is classed as "ExamReady" once they've completed the SKA, the Personal Learning Plan, the practice papers and the mocks, and their working level is above 2.5 for Level 2 (above 1.5 for Level 1). A useful reassurance point on a call: proof the learner won't be going in blind.

## Study guidance

We recommend around 50 hours of study to complete the course, done at the learner's own pace with immediate 24/7 access. When the course is completed, the success rate is 93%.

## Other course features

Our accessibility feature allows a learner to change the view of the course for it to be user-friendly for as many learners as possible. Some examples of what this feature can do (but there are a lot more): change font size, screen color, hide images, add a reader guide, read aloud text to speech features, and more.

Module 5: Maths exam - Open Awards
items.body:
**How the Open Awards maths exam runs.**

## Open Awards maths exam & rules

The Open Awards maths exam is a single 2-hour exam, sat online at home with a human invigilator present throughout. It's split into two sections: 30 minutes non-calculator, then 90 minutes with a calculator.

For the calculator section, the learner can either use their own calculator or the one provided on screen — both are allowed. Throughout the exam they can use pen and paper to work things out, but anything they want marked must be entered on screen; rough workings on paper won't be seen by the examiner. The pass mark is typically around 50–60%.

## Results & invigilation

Open Awards results take 6–16 working days. That's slower than VQA (TQUK) (1–6 working days), so if a learner is working to a tight deadline, factor this in when choosing a board.

How the human invigilator works: Open Awards has a real person invigilating live for the whole exam. The learner receives their exam link on the day, joins, and the invigilator supervises them throughout in real time. It's worth flagging to learners who feel reassured by having a person present rather than being recorded.

items.body:
**How the VQA (TQUK) maths exam runs — our default, fastest board.**

## VQA (TQUK) maths exam & rules

The VQA (TQUK) maths exam is a single 2-hour exam made up of two sections, one calculator and one non-calculator. Unlike Open Awards, there is no time limit on each individual section, so the learner manages the full two hours across both as they wish. The pass mark is typically around 50–60%.

The learner cannot bring their own calculator; an on-screen calculator, protractor and ruler are all provided instead. For notes they are allowed just one piece of plain paper, along with an on-screen notes pop-up in the bottom left, which is not marked. Results come back in 1–6 working days, the fastest of any board. There are only three exam papers in a cycle before the next standardisation, so if a learner sits three times and still needs a resit, they either wait for the next cycle or change exam board.

## Invigilation & exam set-up

VQA (TQUK) uses an automated invigilator: the exam is recorded and reviewed afterwards, with no human present during the sitting. The learner receives their login and exam link by email from [exams@tquk.org](mailto:exams@tquk.org), not from us, so it's worth telling them to look out for it and check their spam folder. Chromebooks work fine for VQA (TQUK) exams, but we advise against Macs, which are often unreliable or not compatible.

items.feedback: TQUK maths is one 2-hour exam with two sections and no individual section time limit — unlike Open Awards, which fixes the split at 30/90.

Module 7: English Exam - The Three Components
items.body:
**Reading, Writing, and SLC: how each runs and the pass marks.**

## The three components and timing

The PFS English exam is made up of three components: Reading, Writing, and SLC (Speaking, Listening and Communication). Reading and Writing are sat together in a single 2-hour sitting, split as 1 hour of reading and 1 hour of writing. The SLC is sat separately, on its own day, and takes around an hour.

## How the SLC works

The SLC is a group call. The learner joins up to four other learners, so there are up to five people in total. Beforehand, they choose their own presentation topic and submit it 7 days ahead of the exam, and they also receive an email 7 days before with a set discussion topic that they don't get to choose. On the day, they deliver a 4–7 minute verbal presentation, and everyone else presents too. It works both ways: the learner is asked questions by the other learners, and must put questions to them in return.

## Rules and pass marks

A dictionary is allowed, but only for the reading section. The pass marks differ by component: around 55% for Reading and Writing, and a full 100% (10 out of 10) for the SLC.

Module 8: English Exam - Board Differences
items.body:
**Where Open Awards and TQUK differ on the SLC, dictionaries, paper, and results.**

## Exam boards

For PFS English, we work with two exam boards: **Open Awards** and VQA (TQUK). A learner sits the same qualification either way, but the practical details differ between the two, and those details are exactly what customers ask about.

## SLC day and time

With Open Awards the Level 2 SLC runs at 09:30 Monday to Friday. With VQA (TQUK) it runs later in the day, at 12:30, but only on Wednesdays and Fridays, and only subject to availability. So Open Awards gives the learner far more scheduling flexibility.

## Dictionaries

Open Awards allows a standard Oxford dictionary for the reading section only — not a thesaurus and not a bilingual dictionary. TQUK also allows a dictionary for the reading section.

## Paper and notes

An Open Awards learner can bring scrap paper. A VQA (TQUK) learner cannot do the same: they get one piece of plain paper for maths only, and none at all for English. In the TQUK English exam there's an on-screen notes pop-up instead, but anything written there is not marked.

## Results

Open Awards takes 6 to 16 working days, counted after each component is sat. VQA (TQUK) is much quicker, returning results in 1 to 6 working days.

Module 9: City & Guilds
items.body:
**When (rarely) to use City & Guilds, and why we advise against it.**

## City & Guilds

Alongside Open Awards and VQA (TQUK), we are also registered with a third board for PFS: City & Guilds. The important thing to know up front is that we advise against using it. We only put a learner with City & Guilds if they specifically need it or ask for it by name — otherwise Open Awards or VQA (TQUK) will almost always serve them better.

## Why we advise against it

Two reasons we steer away. First, the tech test: before sitting the exam the learner must book and pass a separate tech test (downloading software), then wait at least five working days, which delays everything. Second, results take up to 32 working days — far longer than Open Awards (6–16) or VQA (TQUK) (1–6).

## Exam set-up

A few facts for when a learner does choose it. Chromebooks cannot be used and dictionaries are not allowed; however, they can use their own scrap paper. The SLC has three tasks: a presentation on a familiar topic (own topic, signed off by admin), a discussion on an unfamiliar topic (given three options, chosen on the day), and a discussion in response to a short video. The SLC information is sent in an email 7 days before.

Module 10: Access Arrangements
items.body:
**Where evidence goes, how long each board needs, what each grants, and SLC exemption.**

## How it works

We can apply directly with the exam board for extra requirements such as extra time, a reader, or a scribe. What is available differs by board. After booking, the learner sends their evidence to the exams team at [help@passfunctionalskills.co.uk](mailto:help@passfunctionalskills.co.uk) — for example a diagnostic letter, a doctor's letter, or an EHCP. The boards each need time to grant and apply the arrangements before the exam. VQA (TQUK) needs 6 working days and grants only 25% extra time. Open Awards needs 10 working days and offers all access arrangements. City & Guilds needs 20 working days and grants only 25% extra time.

## SLC exemption (English)

In extreme circumstances a learner can be made exempt from the SLC component — for reasons beyond typical access arrangements, such as the learner being mute. This requires full medical evidence: a doctor's note is not accepted, but an EHCP is a good option. If approved, the certificate will state that the SLC element was not completed. We cannot guarantee that universities or courses will accept this, as it is decided case by case, though we have not yet had one refused.

Module 12: Resits
items.body:
**Cycle limits per board, component resits, credit transfer, and the supportive resit-call script and tone.**

## Resits

A learner can retake an exam at any point once they have the results from their previous attempt. How many times they can resit depends on the board. With VQA (TQUK) a learner can resit three times before the next cycle, while Open Awards and City & Guilds allow up to five attempts. After reaching that limit, the learner would need to change exam board if they wanted to retake again within that cycle.

## Component resits

What a learner has to resit depends on the subject. For maths, the learner must sit the whole exam again. For English, they only need to resit the components they have failed — they do not have to redo all three.

English also allows resit components to be taken with different boards, and we can organise a credit transfer to bring them together. The qualification is issued by whichever board holds the majority of the components. For example, if someone passed two components with Open Awards and one with City & Guilds, their qualification would come from Open Awards. One thing to watch: VQA (TQUK) will not issue a component certificate, and will only complete a credit transfer if they hold the majority, meaning two of the three components.

## Resit-call tone

The tone of a resit call matters just as much as the timing. Resit calls are supportive, not salesy. Start by establishing the learner's situation and deadline, reassure them, and lead with support rather than a pitch. The learner has usually just had a setback, so the goal is to help them feel looked after, not sold to.

If a learner needs their results by a certain date, ask what that date is and work back from it, choosing a board whose result turnaround fits the deadline.

Module 13: Entry Level 3 and Digital Skills
items.body:
**What each is, when a learner needs it, and how they sit alongside FS Level 2.**

## Entry Level 3

Entry Level 3 sits below Functional Skills Level 1, and we do not offer it unless a learner specifically asks for it. The courses and exam set-up work in exactly the same way as the standard FS courses. It is available with Open Awards only. The English exam runs as 45 minutes of reading and 50 minutes of writing, and the maths exam is 30 minutes non-calculator followed by 1 hour 15 minutes with a calculator.

## Digital Skills

Digital Functional Skills is a Level 1 course only, and there is no exam to offer with it. It builds practical digital skills for work, study, and everyday life, and it works like the maths and English courses. The learner starts with a Subject Knowledge Assessment, and each topic then has three sections: Revise (interactive walkthroughs and written slides), Practice Questions (multiple choice), and Topic Tests (written answers, AI-marked with feedback and a model answer). There is one full mock paper, which is multiple choice plus written and marked by the Dr Clive AI. Progress tracking shows course progress, current level, and scores, but there is no "Exam Ready" status, because there is no exam.

## Digital Skills pricing

Digital Skills is sold at £99. It can be offered at £49 only if agreed by management beforehand. There is no exam fee, as it is a course only.
